newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo budget and GDP not seen stabilizing economy.
newsitem.headline: Yugo budget and GDP not seen stabilizing economy.

text.p: A group of prominent Yugoslav economists questioned on Friday whether the government was sincerely committed to stabilisation after it proposed a 70 percent rise in its 1997 budget.

The government's draft budget, qualified as restrictive, amounts to 9.238 billion dinars ($1.86 billion) and assumes a healthy 13 percent economy growth, raising the value of gross domestic product (GDP) to 103.28 billion dinars ($20.9 billion).

"The 1997 budget will grow by 70 percent. The government collected 4.177 billion dinars from January to October 1996. If the trend continues, total 1996 budget revenues will be 5.3-5.4 billion dinars," Miroljub Labus of the Economics Institute told a news conference.
According to Labus, the 1997 budget and GDP will produce inflation rate well above 40 percent in 1997.
Both GDP and the budget are estimated on the basis of predicted spending and costs, another economist said.
"Last year they expected a 19 percent growth in GDP and 120 percent annual inflation. Such a high estimate was needed to make up for enormous public spending," said Zoran Popov of the same institute.
Labus insisted the proposed budget would not lead to economic stabilisation. He said budget calculations remained very much the same for the past three years.
"First they overestimate GDP and inflation rate has never been precisely determined. Then, according to a preset key they allocate money to all budget recepients," Labus told Reuters.

"But since those needs are high, allocation of funds leads to pronounced jump in inflation during January and February, far above projected values, forcing them later to apply brakes on budget spending," he said.
GDP is unrealistically estimated at 103 billion dinars or 29 billion German marks, he added.

"We cannot say which part is inflation, but if the 1994 GDP stood at 20.5 billion marks and if you take into account GDP growth rates for 1995 and 1996 and add the assumed 13 percent for 1997, there are three billion German marks left uncovered," Labus said.
According to Labus this represented a portion of inflation or rather some ten percent of the public deficit to be financed from inflation in the course of 1997.
"It's too much and it will reignite inflation, requiring temporary restrictive measures to suppress it. This stop-go policy reacts to short-term needs only."
Economists pointed to public spending retaining a high 47.5 percent share in the GDP.
Popov said the biggest problem is how to reduce public spending. "We all want it, but there are problems. It's a tough decision for politicians and could threaten social peace."
He said a deep cut in public spending needed more time and meant new sources of financing pensions, education and health.
($1 = 1.5029 German marks) -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
